issues.description: The Experiment 1 sample flow is internally impossible. After 45 participants started training and 5 were excluded, 40 should remain. The analysis then states that exclusion for too few high-confidence critical trials resulted in inclusion of 23 participants while only 5 participants were excluded, which cannot both be true. This prevents verification of the analyzed sample size and undermines reproducibility of all Experiment 1 statistics.
issues.quote: 45 participants started training, 5 participants were excluded based on their training results. The remaining 40 participants... Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded)

issues.description: Across experiments, participants were excluded after data collection based on having too few high-confidence trials, including 92/290 participants in Experiment 2 and an unclear but apparently large fraction in Experiment 1. Because confidence is part of the dependent behavior and varies with memory strength, excluding participants on this basis can create selection bias and restrict conclusions to a high-confidence/high-performing subset rather than the sampled population.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded)

issues.description: The primary analyses are conducted only on high-confidence trials. Confidence is measured after the choice and is itself affected by stimulus type, memory delay, task difficulty, and response bias. Conditioning on this post-outcome variable can distort error rates and create collider/selection bias. The manuscript does not present parallel analyses of all trials or model confidence jointly with accuracy, so the reported illusion rates may not represent actual error prevalence.
issues.quote: As in Experiment 1, error rates on high confidence trials were analyzed in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter), memory delay (long or short) and error type (illusions -from pseudo-to-real or the other way around- vs other errors) as independent variables

issues.subcategory: high confidence does not establish false memory
issues.description: The authors equate high-confidence errors with illusory memories and low-confidence errors with guesses. This is not justified. High confidence can arise from response bias, familiarity, demand characteristics, fluency, or miscalibrated metacognition. Without independent measures of subjective recollection, confidence calibration, signal-detection modeling, or phenomenological reports, high confidence alone cannot establish that participants had an actual illusory memory trace.
issues.quote: Illusory memories should result in high confidence erroneous responses, where the participants has access to a memory trace (albeit an incorrect memory trace). In the absence of confidence ratings, the erroneous responses could actually consist of low confidence responses or even outright guesses.

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly analyzes “high confidence” trials but does not clearly state how high confidence was operationalized, especially for the 1–4 confidence scale in Experiments 2–4. Without the exact threshold, the analyses cannot be reproduced and the interpretation of reported error percentages is ambiguous.
issues.quote: After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain).

issues.description: Experiment 1 contains inconsistent descriptions of the confidence scale. The figure caption says confidence was rated from 1 to 4, whereas the procedure says there were only two boxes from 1 to 2. This affects the definition of high-confidence trials and comparability across experiments.
issues.quote: Subsequently she indicated confidence in her judgment (1 = guess, 4 = certainty).

issues.subcategory: delay manipulation confounded with cue timing and report timing
issues.description: The experiments describe the manipulation as memory delay, but participants did not report immediately after the cue. In Experiment 1, the second display appeared 5 seconds after memory-display offset, and only after that did participants respond. Thus the “short” condition involved an early cue followed by a long retention/response interval and an intervening display, while the “long” condition involved a later cue and different cue-to-interference timing. This manipulates retrocue timing, selection, protection from interference, and response maintenance, not simply elapsed time from perception to report.
issues.quote: In all conditions, after offset of the second letter display, the participant first indicated the identity of the letter at the cued location in the memory display.

issues.subcategory: same issue in Experiment 2 delay manipulation
issues.description: Experiment 2 also delays the actual response until after an intervening display presented 3.75 seconds after the memory display. The short condition therefore does not measure memory report at 0.5 seconds; it measures performance after an early cue, subsequent maintenance, and interference. Claims about illusions at 500 ms or increasing from 500 ms to 3 s are therefore not directly supported.
issues.quote: Then the cue was presented for 0.25 seconds... 3.75 seconds after the offset of the memory display, the second display was presented for 0.25 seconds... After this the participant first chose the target letter from 6 different response options

issues.subcategory: increase over time does not rule out perceptual encoding errors
issues.description: The central inference that an increase in errors over delay proves that errors are memory-based is too strong. Perceptual/encoding errors could interact with differential decay, retrieval noise, response bias, or loss of orientation information over time. Delayed increases show that later processes contribute, but they do not show that initial perception was accurate or that memory traces were converted from pseudo to real letters.
issues.quote: This effect must be due to processes ongoing in STM: Had these illusory memories been the result of changes in perception, they should have been present at the earlier probe as well.

issues.description: The study never measures perception while the display is present or immediately at offset without subsequent memory and decision demands. Even the earliest probes occur after the display has disappeared and, in some experiments, before a delayed response after interference. Therefore the manuscript cannot cleanly separate perception, encoding, maintenance, retrieval, and decision stages.
issues.quote: In two conditions the memory probe appeared 0.75 seconds after offset of the memory display, in the third memory condition, the probe appeared 3 seconds after offset of the memory display.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 target often absent from response display
issues.description: In Experiment 1, critical trials often replaced the true target with its mirrored counterpart rather than presenting both. Participants had to choose “none of these” when the correct target was absent. This makes illusion rates dependent on detecting target absence and using the none option, not just on remembering orientation. It also differs from later experiments, limiting comparability.
issues.quote: If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options. If the target was a real letter, then it appeared as a response option on a randomly selected 83% of the trials, while its mirror reversed (pseudo-letter) version appeared as a response option on the other 16% of the trials.

issues.description: The forced-choice response format and higher familiarity of real letters create strong potential for response bias toward real letters. The analyses compare raw selection percentages rather than estimating sensitivity and bias with a signal-detection or multinomial processing model. Therefore pseudo-to-real responses may reflect response preference or familiarity at retrieval rather than altered memory content.
issues.quote: Yet another reason why illusory reports arise could be a response bias: Participant might just be more inclined to select real letters instead of pseudo-letters, since real letters are a well-known category. However, this is unlikely because the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias.

issues.description: The asymmetry between pseudo-to-real and real-to-pseudo errors is interpreted as evidence for world knowledge, but the design also confounds pseudo letters with lower familiarity, lower nameability, weaker verbal encoding, and the need to bind an identity to an orientation/mirror feature. These alternatives can predict the same asymmetry without invoking expectations reshaping memory.
issues.quote: This suggests that world knowledge is a more important driver of illusory memories than visual similarity, as visual similarity between to-be-remembered target and the mirrored counterpart that is presented in the response screen is clearly identical in both cases.

issues.subcategory: orientation-feature loss alternative not ruled out
issues.description: Pseudo-letter trials can be encoded as a real letter identity plus a “mirrored” feature. If the mirror/orientation feature is forgotten while identity remains, participants would choose the real counterpart. This is a feature-binding or verbal-recoding failure, not necessarily an expectation-induced false memory. The experiments do not include controls that distinguish these mechanisms.
issues.quote: FTT does suggest that pseudo-letters have a verbal (the letter itself) and a gist level (“mirrored”) representation, while real letters can be stored purely at the verbal level.

issues.subcategory: flawed dismissal of weak pseudo-letter trace account
issues.description: The authors argue that if pseudo-letter traces were weaker, participants should choose all response options equally. This is incorrect: a weak or lost orientation feature with preserved letter identity would specifically increase selection of the mirrored counterpart, not all items. Thus an important alternative explanation is dismissed using an invalid prediction.
issues.quote: If that were the case, participants remembering a pseudo-letter target (or more accurately, a participant easily forgetting a weakly established representation of a pseudo-letter target) should be selecting all items in the probe display with equal probability, as the representation of the target has been lost.

issues.subcategory: inappropriate analysis of bounded proportion data
issues.description: The main analyses use repeated-measures ANOVAs on aggregated error percentages. These data are bounded proportions with different denominators across participants and cells, especially after conditioning on high confidence. ANOVA on aggregated percentages ignores binomial sampling variance and can misestimate uncertainty. Trial-level logistic or multinomial mixed-effects models would be more appropriate.
issues.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4 , with the factors Target Type (real or pseudo-letter), Memory Delay (short, short with interference and long) and Error Type.

issues.subcategory: ignoring participant and item random effects
issues.description: The analyses aggregate over trials and letter identities, ignoring random variability across specific letters, mirrored forms, locations, and participants. Some letters are likely more confusable or more nameable than others, so treating all observations as exchangeable without item-level random effects can inflate generality beyond the sampled stimuli.
issues.quote: The response display consisted of 6 letters: the target letter... two other randomly selected letters from the memory display, and 3 letters that did not appear in the memory display.

issues.description: The rule excluding participants with 10 or fewer high-confidence critical trials per cell is arbitrary and not justified by a power, precision, or modeling rationale. It may disproportionately remove participants with lower confidence or poorer memory and changes the estimand to a selected subgroup.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 91 participants (4 participants were excluded).

issues.description: The Experiment 2 non-illusory error analysis contains a serious contradiction. The text says Memory Delay is the relevant factor with BFincl = 190 and that target type is not relevant, but Table 4 reports Memory Delay BFincl = 0.064 and Target Type BFincl = 39110.895. This reverses the statistical conclusion and undermines confidence in the reported analyses.
issues.quote: For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor... Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay) but this increase was the same for pseudo- and real letter targets... Table 4... Memory Delay... BFincl... 0.064... Target Type... BFincl... 39110.895

issues.description: Bayes factors depend on prior specifications, especially in Bayesian ANOVA and follow-up t-tests. The manuscript reports Bayes factors from JASP but does not specify the prior distributions, scale parameters, model-prior settings, or sensitivity analyses. This limits reproducibility and interpretability of the Bayesian evidence.
issues.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4

issues.description: Experiments 3 and 4 used sequential Bayes-factor stopping, but the stopping rule is only loosely described and is based on a “critical t-test” whereas the primary reported analyses are ANOVAs. The prior for the sequential test, exact monitoring schedule, maximum sample size, and handling of optional stopping are not fully specified, making the evidential strength hard to evaluate.
issues.quote: Sample size was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t-test, namely the comparison between the effect of Error-Type for Real and Pseudo-letter targets. Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop.

issues.subcategory: no prospective sample-size justification for key experiments
issues.description: Experiment 2’s sample size was determined by course enrollment rather than a planned power or precision analysis. Experiment 1 also lacks a clear sample-size rationale. This makes it difficult to know whether null results, such as the cue-color manipulation, are interpretable and whether the experiments were designed to estimate effects with adequate precision.
issues.quote: The number of participants was determined not by the experimenter but by student enrollment in the course, which explains the large increase in participants compared to Experiment 1.

issues.subcategory: multiple follow-up tests without correction or hierarchy
issues.description: The manuscript conducts multiple model comparisons, follow-up ANOVAs, and follow-up t-tests across experiments without a clearly prespecified testing hierarchy or adjustment for multiplicity. This increases the risk of selective emphasis and makes the evidential interpretation of secondary effects less secure.
issues.quote: Follow-up ANOVAs conducted separately for each error type showed that for illusory errors... For other, non-illusory errors... BF > 1000 in follow-up t-test

issues.description: The 'other errors' comparison category pools different response types, including non-target memory items, new distractors, and possibly mirrored counterparts of other items. These alternatives differ in memory status and similarity to the target. Comparing the mirrored-target error to this heterogeneous aggregate does not isolate an illusion process cleanly.
issues.quote: For each memory delay (short, short with interference and long) and each target type (pseudo- and real letter targets) the occurrence of illusory errors (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) and other errors (selection of one of the unrelated distractor items) was calculated.

issues.subcategory: interfering display may create source confusion
issues.description: The irrelevant second display contains letters and pseudo-letters and is presented before response. It could introduce source-monitoring errors, overwrite visual features, prime real-letter choices, or cause participants to select items from the second display. The analyses do not report whether erroneous responses corresponded to items in the intervening display.
issues.quote: To increase memory decay through task-irrelevant interference, a second display was included in each trial. This display consisted of randomly selected letters, unrelated to the memory display. Participants were instructed to ignore this second display.

issues.subcategory: trial feedback can induce learning and strategy changes
issues.description: Participants received feedback after trials and blocks despite the study aiming to distinguish lifelong world knowledge from experiment-induced expectations and response strategies. Feedback may teach base rates, emphasize real/pseudo distinctions, or alter confidence and response criteria over time. No learning, block, or fatigue analyses are reported.
issues.quote: After each trial the participant received feedback (correct/ incorrect response) on her performance. The main experiment consisted of 12 blocks of 20 trials. After each block the participant received feedback on her performance which included information about her average accuracy.

issues.description: Experiment 1 allowed only participants exceeding 75% on a separate visual memory training task to enter the main experiment. This selects for motivated/high-performing participants and may change the prevalence of confidence and errors relative to the general population. The consequences of this selection are not assessed.
issues.quote: Participants could only participate in the actual experiment, if they scored higher than 75% correct (averaged across all trials) on the final 10 blocks of training.

issues.description: Critical visual properties of the letters are not fully specified, including font, case, exact letter size, stroke width, anti-aliasing, and monitor parameters. Because mirror discrimination and letter familiarity depend strongly on typography and display characteristics, this limits replicability and may affect the magnitude of the reported illusions.
issues.quote: The memory and cue displays were set up in the same way as the displays in the training session, with 6 or 8 letters replacing the tilted bars. Pseudo-letter were mirrored (i.e. flipped from left to right).

issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online on participants' own laptops. A 250 ms memory display and 500 ms/3000 ms intervals require accurate timing and visual-angle control, but the manuscript provides no calibration, browser/hardware timing validation, screen-size control, viewing-distance control, or exclusion based on timing failures. This threatens comparability with lab experiments and interpretation of short-delay effects.
issues.quote: the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting . Participants... were given the link to the Neurotask experiment, which they then started on their own laptop.

issues.description: Experiment 2’s cue-color manipulation is interpreted as having no effect, but the reported initial analysis includes only target type and cue color for illusory errors and omits memory delay and other error types. If cue effects depend on delay or alter confidence/response bias rather than only illusion rates, this analysis could miss them. Collapsing over cue color may obscure theoretically relevant interactions.
issues.quote: First, we tested whether the cue colour influenced the occurrence of illusory errors, analysing the illusory error rates (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter) and cue colour (red or blue, indicating low and high probability of a pseudoletter target) as factors. Since this analysis showed no effects of cue colour... the rest of the analysis was conducted while collapsing over the two cue colour conditions.

issues.subcategory: cue color confounded with luminance and probability
issues.description: The red and blue cue colors differed substantially in luminance as well as in target-type probability. Any cue effect, or absence of one, could be influenced by perceptual salience or attentional capture rather than learned expectation. The manuscript does not report counterbalancing color-probability assignments across participants.
issues.quote: both the central fixation cross and the cue were either blue (CIE: 0.148, 0.078, luminance: 6.47 cd/m2) or red (CIE: 0.641, 0.341; luminance: 11.9 cd/m2)... If the fixation cross and the cue were red, a pseudo-letter was the target on 25% of the trials. The target was a pseudo-letter on 60% of the trials when the fixation cross and the cue were blue.

issues.description: The conclusion that the transient cue-probability manipulation failed because expectations need substantial time to develop is not warranted. The only reported awareness check was a brief post-experiment questionnaire, and absence of spontaneous mention does not show participants failed to learn the contingency or that implicit expectations were absent.
issues.quote: Participants filled out a brief questionnaire in which they were invited to indicate what the experiment was about after the experiment. The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses.

issues.description: The manuscript infers from a null cue-color effect that expectations require substantial time to develop. This is an overinterpretation because the manipulation may have been too weak, unnoticed, confounded by color/luminance, or analyzed with insufficient sensitivity to interactions.
issues.quote: However, transiently generated expectations, in this case provided by a cue about the prevalence of real versus pseudo-letters targets, had no effect on the prevalence of illusory memories. This is consistent with the notion that expectations need substantial time to develop before they can affect explicit, high confidence memories.

issues.description: Statements such as pseudo-to-real illusions being almost as frequent as correct selections are based only on high-confidence trials, after excluding many participants and trials. They should not be interpreted as the probability that memory is illusory overall. The manuscript sometimes presents these conditional percentages in a way that may overstate prevalence.
issues.quote: high confidence pseudo-to-real illusions (43%) were almost as prevalent as high confidence selections of the actual pseudo-target (50%). That is, when participants were sure of their memory, the recollection was almost as likely to be illusory as it was to be real.

issues.description: The general discussion states that memory was probed at 500 ms in Experiments 1 and 2, but Experiment 1’s short cue was 0.75 s, and in both experiments actual responses occurred later after intervening displays. The timing claim is therefore inaccurate and overstates the immediacy of the measured reports.
issues.quote: Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2) and up to 30% of reports when memory is probed at 3 seconds (Experiment 1-4).

issues.description: The manuscript frames the findings as showing that STM in general is susceptible to false memories. However, all experiments use a highly specific task involving mirror-reversed letters, verbal labels, and orientation judgments. The results may not generalize to STM broadly or to non-symbolic visual memory.
issues.quote: Here, we present 4 studies that explore whether STM in general is susceptible to false memories just like LTM has been shown to be.

issues.description: The data are compatible with several mechanisms, including response bias, feature-binding failure, verbal recoding, differential discriminability, and source confusion. The manuscript's claim that the findings support a predictive-processing account is plausible but not uniquely tested by the experiments.
issues.quote: Our findings support a predictive processing view of the formation and maintenance of memory in which all memory stages, including STM, involve integration of bottom-up memory input with top-down predictions, such that prior expectations can shape memory traces.

issues.subcategory: possible participant overlap across experiments not fully addressed
issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states that Experiment 2 participants did not take part in Experiment 1, but comparable exclusions for overlap among Experiments 2, 3, and 4 are not clearly reported despite all drawing from first-year psychology participants. Non-independence could affect claims of replication across experiments.
issues.quote: All participants were naïve to the purpose of this experiment and did not take part in Experiment 1.

issues.description: The Experiment 4 results refer to Figure 5 even though the Experiment 4 figure is labeled Figure 6. This is a minor reporting error but indicates insufficient proofreading and can confuse readers.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials... Figure 6 Experiment 4.

issues.description: The manuscript contains several typographical and terminology errors, including inconsistent spelling/capitalization of Bayes-factor notation and 'pseudoletter' versus 'pseudo-letter'. While minor individually, these issues can obscure statistical reporting and should be corrected.
issues.quote: BFinlc>1000
